content: In settings with limited access to laboratory infrastructure and testing, or in populations where rapid testing can facilitate linkage to care and treatment, the use of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) is strongly recommended, despite the evidence being of low to moderate quality. For adults and children older than 18 months, it is recommended to use a single serological assay to detect evidence of past or present infection before conducting supplementary nucleic acid testing (NAT) to confirm viraemic infection. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. To diagnose viraemic infection, it is recommended to use quantitative or qualitative NAT to detect HCV RNA immediately after a reactive HCV antibody serological test result. This is the preferred strategy and is strongly recommended, although the evidence quality is moderate to low. Alternatively, an assay to detect HCV core antigen (p22), which has comparable clinical sensitivity to NAT, can be used as a conditional recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. HCV infection in children under 18 months can only be confirmed using virological assays to detect HCV RNA. This is because maternal antibodies transferred through the placenta remain in the child’s bloodstream until 18 months of age, making serological test results ambiguous. Laboratory-based immunoassays, such as enzyme immunoassay (EIA), chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA), and electrochemiluminescence assay (ECL), should meet minimum acceptance criteria, such as WHO prequalification or stringent regulatory review for in vitro diagnostics (IVDs). All IVDs should be used according to manufacturers’ instructions and, where possible, at testing sites enrolled in national or international external quality assessment schemes. An assay suitable for point-of-care use or dried blood spot (DBS) specimens, with a detection limit of 3000 IU/mL or lower, is acceptable. Such an assay would identify 95% of individuals with viraemic infection based on available data. Screening for alcohol use and providing counseling to reduce moderate to high levels of alcohol intake is strongly recommended for all individuals with HCV infection. This recommendation is based on moderate-quality evidence. In resource-limited settings, the aminotransferase/platelet ratio index (APRI) or FIB-4 tests are suggested for assessing hepatic fibrosis, as they require fewer resources compared to elastography or FibroTest. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. For individuals with HCV genotype 3 infection who have previously received interferon and/or ribavirin, a 16-week treatment duration is recommended. In countries where genotype distribution is well-known and genotype 3 prevalence is less than 5%, this approach may be considered. However, treatment in adolescents still requires genotyping to determine the appropriate regimen. The objective of these guidelines is to provide updated, evidence-based recommendations for the care and treatment of individuals with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, including when to treat and what treatments to use for children, adolescents, and adults. These guidelines aim to support policymakers, clinicians, and implementing partners in developing or updating national hepatitis policies and treatment guidelines. The global burden of HCV infection is significant, with an estimated 71 million people living with chronic HCV infection in 2015, resulting in 399,000 deaths from cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). HCV infection also contributes to comorbidities such as depression, diabetes mellitus, and chronic renal disease, some of which are directly attributable to HCV. The introduction of safe, highly effective, and well-tolerated direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens has transformed the treatment landscape for chronic HCV infection. These regimens achieve high cure rates and are now recommended for all individuals with chronic HCV infection, regardless of fibrosis stage. The availability of pangenotypic DAA regimens has reduced the need for genotyping, and the substantial reduction in DAA prices has enabled rapid treatment rollout in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). The World Health Organization (WHO) aims to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030, defined as a 90% reduction in new chronic infections and a 65% reduction in mortality compared to 2015 levels. Achieving these targets requires diagnosing 90% of those infected and treating 80% of those diagnosed. However, significant gaps remain in service coverage, with only 7% of infected individuals having started treatment as of 2015. HCV infection can lead to both acute and chronic hepatitis. While 15–45% of individuals clear the virus spontaneously within six months, the remaining 55–85% develop chronic infection, which can progress to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and HCC. Risk factors for disease progression include alcohol use, HBV or HIV coinfection, and immunosuppression. HCV infection is also associated with extrahepatic manifestations, including depression, diabetes, and chronic renal disease. These comorbidities are likely to be affected by treatment, and their prevalence is generally independent of liver fibrosis severity. HIV/HCV coinfection accelerates the progression of HCV-related liver disease, including cirrhosis and HCC. Coinfected individuals, particularly those with advanced immunodeficiency, experience more rapid disease progression compared to those with HCV monoinfection. In high-income countries, HCV-associated liver disease is a leading cause of death among people living with HIV. HCV transmission occurs through unsafe healthcare practices, injecting drug use, and, less frequently, sexual contact. Unsafe healthcare-associated practices, such as unsterilized injections and unscreened blood transfusions, remain significant drivers of HCV transmission in some countries. Addressing these issues requires safer healthcare practices, the use of reuse-prevention devices, and a reduction in unnecessary injections. Pangenotypic DAA regimens, such as sofosbuvir/velpatasvir and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, have demonstrated high efficacy across all major HCV genotypes, including in individuals with cirrhosis or HIV coinfection. These regimens are now widely recommended for treating HCV infection. Access to DAAs has improved significantly due to the availability of low-cost generic medicines, particularly in LMICs. This has facilitated the rapid expansion of treatment programs and supports the goal of eliminating HCV as a public health threat.
